analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel companies for carbon emissions and divides the money equally among all Americans as quarterly dividends.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap carbon emissions and pay every American a share of the auction proceeds died in committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies that produce or import oil, coal, and natural gas to buy a limited number of carbon permits at public auctions, with the amount shrinking each year until emissions were 90% below 2015 levels by 2050. All the auction money would go into a trust fund that pays an equal dividend to every eligible American each quarter — the idea being that higher fuel costs would be offset by the dividend, which pays out most for lower-income households who use less energy. It also included border fees on carbon-intensive imports, environmental justice monitoring, and protection for climate-related lawsuits against fossil fuel companies. The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every eligible U.S. resident with a valid Social Security number would receive an equal, tax-free quarterly dividend funded entirely by the fossil fuel auction proceeds. Because the dividend is the same for everyone, it is proportionally largest for lower- and middle-income households, who generally use less energy than the wealthy. It would also benefit communities near polluting facilities through air quality monitoring and additional protections if local pollution does not fall alongside carbon emissions, and U.S. manufacturers of carbon-intensive goods through border fees on imports that lack equivalent carbon costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary households receiving equal climate dividends

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies that produce or import oil, coal, and natural gas to buy a shrinking annual supply of carbon permits at auction, with a $40-per-ton minimum price rising by $10 each year, cutting emissions 90% below 2015 levels by 2050.
Sends all auction proceeds and penalties to a Healthy Climate Trust Fund, which pays each lawful resident with a Social Security number an equal quarterly dividend, tax-free.

Includes environmental justice provisions: air quality monitoring in frontline communities and authority to impose additional measures if local co-pollutant pollution does not fall alongside carbon emissions.
Imposes border fees on carbon-intensive imports (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, and similar goods) and rebates exporters, so U.S. producers are not undercut by countries without carbon rules.
Preserves the right of states, cities, and individuals to sue fossil fuel companies over climate deception and damage.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of crude oil, coal, and natural gas would pay for carbon permits at auction, with a minimum price of $40 per ton rising $10 each year plus inflation, plus triple-damages penalties for noncompliance. Those costs would largely be passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity — though the equal dividend is designed to more than offset that increase for most households, since higher-income households use more energy on average.

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel companies would pass the cost of permits through to consumers, raising prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, particularly during the years before and alongside dividend payments.

The bill sets an aggressive emissions schedule — 90% below 2015 levels by 2050 with a $40-per-ton floor rising $10 a year — which critics would call economically disruptive for energy-intensive regions and industries.
The carbon equivalency fee on imported steel, aluminum, cement, and other goods would raise prices for imported manufactured products and could provoke trade retaliation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have been large and broad: a binding cap on the main driver of climate change and a dividend that for most households would exceed the higher fuel prices it causes. The costs are real: fossil fuel producers and importers would pay tens of billions of dollars a year, and those costs would be passed through to anyone who drives, heats a home, or buys goods made with energy, hitting lower-income and rural households hardest even after dividends (which start only after the first auction) are counted. Critics could also argue the 2050 target assumes technology that does not yet exist at scale, and that border fees could spark trade disputes. But the design — full auction, price floor, equal per-person dividends, no permit giveaways — addresses the most common objections to carbon pricing. The bill's fatal weakness was political, not technical: it never attracted a single cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of a Congress ending in two weeks, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Van Hollen introduced the bill on December 21, 2022, in the final days of the 117th Congress.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the chamber's standard first step.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and no committee or floor action followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies and other large emitters are better off, because they never faced a binding emissions cap or the cost of buying permits; ordinary people gained nothing, since the dividends never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies avoiding a carbon price

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee in the final two weeks of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 21, 2022 and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Fossil fuel and utility interests
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed carbon-pricing legislation that charges producers for emissions; no such campaign appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no votes, no partisan shape can be read from the record; the only observable support was a single Democratic senator.

industries.industry: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: They would have had to buy a shrinking pool of carbon permits each year, with a rising price floor, directly cutting into the profitability of fossil fuel production and import. No permits were given away for free, unlike some earlier cap-and-trade designs.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: They would pay more for energy, but border fees on comparable imports and rebates for exports would offset the cost of competing against countries without carbon rules.
A rising, predictable carbon price would have made wind, solar, and other low-carbon energy relatively cheaper than fossil fuels, accelerating investment in the sector.
